title: The march to Tabuk
hook: a long march in the heat, and three who stayed behind and told the truth (9:117–118)

segments.voice: Yesterday, sakinah: the calm sent down to the ones who stood, when the biggest army yet nearly broke at Hunayn. Your line was numbers didn't help.

In the summer heat, the Prophet ﷺ called for a long march north to Tabuk, near the Byzantine frontier. Ka'b's own account says it came at a hard moment: fierce heat, a long distance, and the fruit in Medina just ripening, the shade at its best. A large army went. Some stayed home and later came with excuses. And one man, Ka'b ibn Malik, a veteran who had no excuse at all, kept telling himself he'd catch up tomorrow, and tomorrow, until the army was too far away. Missing something is one thing. Explaining it is another. The easy excuse is always right there: the car, the sick kid, the dead phone.
screen: `A MARCH IN FIERCE HEAT.` → `SOME CAME BACK WITH EXCUSES.` → `KA'B KEPT SAYING TOMORROW.`

segments.voice: Sahih al-Bukhari keeps Ka'b's account in his own voice, told years later. When the army returned, the people who had stayed behind lined up with their excuses, more than eighty of them, the report says, and the Prophet accepted what they said on the surface and left their hearts to God. Then it was Ka'b's turn. He was a good talker, he said later, and could have walked out of there with a story. Instead he told the truth: I had no excuse. I was never stronger or better off than when I stayed behind. The Prophet said: this one has told the truth. Two others, Murarah and Hilal, said the same. Then came the hard part. For fifty days, the community was told not to speak to the three. Ka'b would greet the Prophet and watch to see if his lips moved in reply. His cousin wouldn't answer him. The ninth surah describes it: the earth, vast as it was, became narrow for them, and their own souls felt narrow, until they understood there was no refuge from God except in Him. Then the verses came down: God had turned to them in forgiveness. Ka'b said afterward that the greatest blessing of his life, after Islam itself, was that he didn't lie that day. And the surah adds a line, in Pickthall's words: "be with the truthful."
screen: `KA'B TELLS IT HIMSELF.` · `I HAD NO EXCUSE.` · `FIFTY DAYS OF SILENCE.` · `GOD TURNED TO THEM.` · then, large: `BE WITH THE TRUTHFUL.`

segments.voice: Think of a small excuse you've been using: the reason you gave for missing something, the version of events that's a little kinder to you than it should be. Name the true version to yourself, plainly, the way Ka'b did: I had no excuse. If you pray, you can say it to God; if there's a person you owe the truth to, just notice who it is.
Sidq, truthfulness: what the three who stayed behind from the march to Tabuk told, even when it cost them fifty hard days.
Your line: the truth saved them. Fifty hard days, and then forgiveness. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Muslims read Ka'b ibn Malik's account in the hadith collections as a model of repentance through honesty, and 9:119, be with the truthful, is often quoted in sermons on truthfulness.

chat.says: Why did Ka'b admit he had no excuse for missing the march to Tabuk?
options: He chose the truth over an easy story, and called it his life's blessing.
He knew the Prophet turned down everyone else's excuses anyway.
He thought owning up would spare him any hard consequences.
chat.meaning: Ka'b could have talked his way out, but said: I had no excuse. After fifty hard days, God turned to them in forgiveness.
